questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The State, as a political concept, is best defined as
options: a religious institution with global membership
a group of people who share the same language and culture
a political community occupying a definite territory, organised under a sovereign government
any organisation formed to trade for profit
questions.explanation: A State possesses four key elements: a defined population, territory, government, and sovereignty, distinguishing it from other social or cultural groupings.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Sovereignty refers to the
options: total population living within a country
official currency used within a country
supreme and final authority of a State to govern itself without external interference
geographical boundary separating two countries
questions.explanation: Sovereignty is the highest, unchallenged authority a State exercises over its territory and people, both internally (supreme over its citizens) and externally (independent of other states).

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A Nation differs from a State mainly in that a Nation is based primarily on
options: a formally established government structure
a shared sense of identity, culture, language, or history among a people
a fixed and legally recognised territorial boundary
international diplomatic recognition
questions.explanation: A Nation is a socio-cultural concept based on shared identity and common bonds among a people, which may or may not align with the political/legal boundaries of a State.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Political power refers to the
options: ability to influence or control the behaviour of others, especially in governance
amount of wealth possessed by an individual
number of political parties in a country
physical strength of a country's military alone
questions.explanation: Power in the political sense is the capacity to make others act (or refrain from acting) in a particular way, often to achieve political or governmental objectives.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Political authority differs from mere power mainly in that authority is
options: power exercised without any form of recognition or consent
unrelated to any legal or constitutional basis
power obtained purely through military force
power that is recognised as rightful and legitimate by those over whom it is exercised
questions.explanation: Authority is power accepted as legitimate and rightful, typically because it is derived from law, tradition, or the consent of the governed, unlike raw, unrecognised coercive power.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Legitimacy in government refers to the
options: widespread acceptance by citizens that a government's authority to rule is rightful
amount of foreign aid a country receives
physical size of a country's territory
number of years a leader has been in power
questions.explanation: Legitimacy exists when the majority of citizens accept and recognise a government's right to exercise authority, often based on lawful processes such as free and fair elections.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Democracy, as a political ideology, is best described as a system of government
options: controlled entirely by a single hereditary ruler
run exclusively by unelected military officers
by the people, in which citizens exercise power directly or through elected representatives
in which one political party permanently holds all power by force
questions.explanation: Democracy is founded on the principle of popular sovereignty, where political power ultimately derives from the people, exercised through free elections and representative institutions.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Capitalism, as an economic and political ideology, is characterised mainly by
options: the complete abolition of private property
central planning of all economic activities by the government
state ownership and control of all means of production
private ownership of the means of production and a free market economy
questions.explanation: Capitalism emphasises private enterprise and market-driven economic decisions, with limited government intervention, contrasting with socialism's emphasis on collective or state ownership.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Socialism, as a political ideology, advocates for
options: unrestricted private ownership of all economic resources
the complete absence of any government
the concentration of power in a single hereditary monarch
collective or state ownership of the means of production to promote social equality
questions.explanation: Socialism seeks to reduce inequality by having the means of production owned or heavily regulated collectively or by the state, rather than left entirely to private individuals.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Fascism, as a political ideology, is generally characterised by
options: an emphasis on individual liberty above all state interests
the complete decentralisation of all governmental authority
extreme nationalism, dictatorial power, and suppression of political opposition
a strong commitment to multi-party democratic elections
questions.explanation: Fascism is typically marked by authoritarian, one-party rule, intense nationalism, and the forcible suppression of dissent and opposing political viewpoints.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A monarchy is a system of government in which supreme power is held by
options: a single ruler, often inherited through a royal family line
an assembly of elected representatives
the military high command
a council of wealthy citizens only
questions.explanation: Monarchies are typically headed by a king, queen, or emperor whose position is usually hereditary, passed down within a royal family.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: An oligarchy is a system of government in which power is concentrated in the hands of
options: the entire adult population through direct voting
an independent judiciary alone
a single absolute ruler
a small group of privileged individuals or families
questions.explanation: Oligarchy describes rule by a small, often wealthy or powerful elite group, rather than by a single individual (autocracy) or the broader population (democracy).

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: An autocracy is a system of government in which
options: power rests solely with a religious council
citizens directly vote on every single law
power is shared equally among several elected bodies
absolute power is concentrated in a single individual, unchecked by other institutions
questions.explanation: In an autocracy, one person holds unrestricted power over the state, without meaningful checks from a legislature, judiciary, or electorate.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: An aristocracy is a system of government in which power is held by
options: the majority of ordinary citizens
a hereditary privileged class considered to be of superior social rank
an appointed group of foreign advisors
a single elected president
questions.explanation: Aristocracy is rule by a hereditary nobility or privileged upper class, historically believed (by supporters) to be best suited to govern due to birth or social standing.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A unitary system of government is one in which
options: power is constitutionally divided between a central government and regional/state governments
each region operates as a fully independent sovereign state
governmental power is centralised in a single national government
there is no central government of any kind
questions.explanation: In a unitary system, ultimate authority rests with the central government, which may delegate some functions to local units, but retains the power to alter or revoke such delegation at will.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A federal system of government is characterised by
options: complete concentration of all power in local governments only
a constitutional division of powers between a central government and constituent states/regions
the merging of several independent countries into one without any internal divisions
the total absence of a central government
questions.explanation: Federalism divides governmental powers constitutionally between a central (federal) authority and regional (state) governments, each with its own defined areas of jurisdiction, as in Nigeria and the USA.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A confederal system of government is best described as one in which
options: regional governments have no independent powers whatsoever
all power is completely centralised in a single national government
the military permanently controls all governmental functions
independent states unite loosely for specific common purposes, while retaining most of their sovereignty
questions.explanation: In a confederation, sovereign states voluntarily cooperate on limited shared matters (like defence or trade), while each member state retains a very high degree of independent authority.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A presidential system of government is characterised mainly by
options: the fusion of executive and legislative powers in a single body
a monarch serving as both head of state and head of government
a clear separation of powers, with an executive president elected independently of the legislature
the complete absence of a legislative body
questions.explanation: In a presidential system, the president (head of the executive) is elected separately from the legislature and serves a fixed term, with powers constitutionally separated from the legislative and judicial branches.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A parliamentary system of government is characterised mainly by
options: an absolute monarch holding all governmental power
a strict separation of powers between all three arms of government
a fusion of executive and legislative powers, with the executive (Prime Minister and Cabinet) drawn from and accountable to the legislature
an executive president elected directly by the people, separate from parliament
questions.explanation: In a parliamentary system, the executive branch (led by a Prime Minister) emerges from and remains accountable to the legislature (parliament), unlike the separated presidential model.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The Legislature, as an organ of government, is primarily responsible for
options: making laws for the country
implementing and enforcing the laws
commanding the armed forces
interpreting and applying the laws
questions.explanation: The legislative arm (e.g., the National Assembly in Nigeria) is constitutionally charged with the primary responsibility of enacting laws for the governance of the state.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The Executive, as an organ of government, is primarily responsible for
options: making all the laws of the country
implementing and enforcing the laws made by the Legislature
interpreting the constitutionality of laws
solely representing the interests of the judiciary
questions.explanation: The executive arm (headed by the President or Prime Minister) is responsible for the day-to-day administration and enforcement of laws and government policy.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The Judiciary, as an organ of government, is primarily responsible for
options: making new laws for the country
interpreting the laws and administering justice
enforcing laws through the police and military
collecting taxes on behalf of government
questions.explanation: The judicial arm interprets and applies the law to resolve disputes and administer justice, while also often reviewing the constitutionality of laws and executive actions.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The doctrine of Separation of Powers advocates that
options: only the Executive should have any real power
the Judiciary should be controlled entirely by the Legislature
all governmental power should be concentrated in a single arm of government
the three arms of government (Legislature, Executive, Judiciary) should be constitutionally distinct and independent of one another
questions.explanation: This doctrine, associated with Montesquieu, holds that dividing governmental power among three separate branches prevents the excessive concentration of power and protects individual liberty.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The system of Checks and Balances is designed to ensure that
options: one arm of government has absolute and unchecked authority over the others
the Legislature has no oversight function over the Executive
each arm of government can monitor and limit the powers of the other arms, preventing abuse of power
the three arms of government never interact with one another
questions.explanation: Checks and balances complement separation of powers by giving each branch specific tools (e.g., veto, impeachment, judicial review) to restrain the others, preventing any single branch from becoming too powerful.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A bicameral legislature is one that consists of
options: no formal chamber structure at all
a single chamber or house only
two chambers or houses, such as a Senate and a House of Representatives
three separate chambers of equal power
questions.explanation: Bicameral legislatures, like Nigeria's National Assembly (Senate and House of Representatives), are divided into two separate legislative chambers, often to provide additional checks on lawmaking.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A unicameral legislature is one that consists of
options: three or more legislative chambers
two separate legislative chambers
no legislative body at all
a single legislative chamber or house
questions.explanation: A unicameral system has just one legislative house, unlike bicameral systems, which divide legislative functions between two chambers.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Judicial independence refers to the principle that
options: the judiciary should have no power to interpret the constitution
courts should be directly controlled by the ruling political party
the judiciary should be free from undue influence or control by the executive or legislature
judges should always agree with the decisions of the executive branch
questions.explanation: Judicial independence ensures that courts can make impartial decisions based on law and fact, free from political pressure or interference from the other arms of government.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The power of judicial review allows the courts to
options: create entirely new laws independent of the legislature
directly appoint members of the executive cabinet
control the day-to-day administration of government ministries
examine and declare the actions or laws of the executive or legislature unconstitutional if they violate the constitution
questions.explanation: Judicial review empowers courts to assess whether laws or governmental actions comply with the constitution, striking down those found to be unconstitutional, reinforcing checks and balances.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Citizenship refers to the legal status of an individual as a
options: temporary visitor to a foreign country
recognised member of a particular State, with accompanying rights and duties
member of an international organisation only
employee of a foreign government
questions.explanation: Citizenship establishes a formal, legal bond between an individual and a State, granting the individual certain rights while also imposing corresponding civic duties.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Citizenship can generally be acquired through which of the following means?
options: Only by winning a national lottery
Only through military conscription
Only by paying a large sum of money to the government
Birth, naturalisation, and registration
questions.explanation: The most common recognised methods of acquiring citizenship are by birth (within a territory or to citizen parents), naturalisation (after meeting residency and legal requirements), and registration.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Citizenship by birth typically applies to a person who is born
options: exclusively to children of foreign diplomats
in any country, regardless of their parents' nationality
within the territory of a State, or to parents who are citizens of that State
only to individuals over the age of eighteen
questions.explanation: Citizenship by birth is usually granted based on either being born within a country's territory (jus soli) or being born to citizen parents regardless of birthplace (jus sanguinis).

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of the following is a duty typically expected of a citizen?
options: Receiving unconditional financial support from the government
Owning property in more than one country
Holding public office without being elected
Obeying the laws of the country and paying taxes
questions.explanation: In exchange for the rights citizenship confers, citizens are typically expected to fulfil civic duties such as obeying laws, paying taxes, and sometimes voting or serving on juries.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Fundamental Human Rights refer to
options: benefits available exclusively to citizens of wealthy nations
rights that can be freely revoked by any private business
basic rights and freedoms guaranteed to every individual, often enshrined in a country's constitution
privileges granted only to elected government officials
questions.explanation: Fundamental human rights (e.g., right to life, freedom of expression, freedom of association) are considered inherent and essential, typically protected explicitly under a nation's constitution.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The right to freedom of expression allows citizens to
options: control what other citizens are allowed to say
avoid ever being criticised by others
say anything at all with absolutely no legal limitations whatsoever
hold and express opinions and ideas without undue government interference
questions.explanation: Freedom of expression protects individuals' rights to voice opinions and ideas, though in practice it is often subject to reasonable legal limitations (e.g., against defamation or incitement to violence).

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Fundamental human rights, though broadly guaranteed, are generally subject to certain limitations mainly to
options: prevent any citizen from ever voting
eliminate the rights of specific ethnic groups
protect public order, national security, and the rights of others
allow the government unlimited power over its citizens
questions.explanation: Most constitutions permit reasonable, legally justified restrictions on rights when necessary to protect public safety, national security, public order, or the rights and freedoms of others.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A political party is best defined as an organised group that
options: operates exclusively outside the electoral process
seeks to gain and exercise governmental power through winning elections
exists solely to provide charitable services to the public
represents only the interests of a single private business
questions.explanation: Political parties are organisations formed with the primary goal of contesting elections to gain control of government and implement their policy agenda.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A one-party system of government is characterised by
options: multiple political parties competing freely in elections
the complete absence of any political party
regular alternation of power between two dominant parties
the existence of only a single legally recognised political party
questions.explanation: In a one-party system, only one political party is permitted to exist or hold power legally, often restricting political competition and pluralism.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A multi-party system of government is characterised by
options: exactly two political parties dominating all elections
only one political party being legally allowed to exist
the complete absence of elections
the existence of three or more political parties competing for power
questions.explanation: Multi-party systems allow several political parties to compete for power and represent diverse viewpoints, distinguishing them from one-party or strictly two-party systems.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Universal adult suffrage refers to the
options: right of all adult citizens who meet basic legal requirements to vote in elections
right to vote granted only to men
practice of appointing, rather than electing, government officials
right to vote granted only to wealthy landowners
questions.explanation: Universal adult suffrage guarantees the right to vote to all adult citizens, regardless of gender, wealth, or social status, subject only to basic requirements like age and citizenship.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The First-Past-The-Post electoral system determines a winner as the candidate who
options: is selected directly by the incumbent government
receives more than fifty percent of the total votes cast
receives the highest number of votes in a constituency, regardless of whether it is an absolute majority
is chosen by a council of traditional rulers
questions.explanation: Under First-Past-The-Post, the candidate with the most votes (a simple plurality) in a constituency wins, even without securing an outright majority of all votes cast.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Proportional representation is an electoral system in which
options: seats are allocated to parties in proportion to the total number of votes they receive
only the candidate with the most votes nationwide wins a single seat
seats are distributed equally regardless of votes received
voting is restricted to members of the ruling party
questions.explanation: Proportional representation aims to more accurately reflect the overall voting pattern of the electorate by distributing legislative seats in line with each party's share of the total vote.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: An Electoral Commission is primarily responsible for
options: enacting the laws that govern the country
administering the country's judicial system
commanding the country's armed forces
organising, conducting, and supervising elections in a country
questions.explanation: Electoral commissions (such as INEC in Nigeria) are independent bodies tasked with managing the electoral process to ensure elections are conducted fairly and transparently.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A pressure group differs from a political party mainly in that a pressure group
options: is formally registered as a branch of government
seeks to influence government policy without directly seeking to win elections or govern
has no interest in influencing public policy at all
always seeks to contest and win elections
questions.explanation: Pressure groups (e.g., trade unions, professional associations) aim to influence government decisions and policies on specific issues, without themselves seeking to hold governmental power through elections.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Public opinion refers to the
options: views expressed exclusively by foreign governments
official position of the ruling political party alone
collective views and attitudes of the general population on political and social issues
personal opinion of a single government minister
questions.explanation: Public opinion represents the aggregate viewpoint of citizens on issues of public concern, which can significantly influence government policy and electoral outcomes.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of the following best distinguishes a pressure group from public opinion as forces influencing government?
options: A pressure group is an organised body, while public opinion is a more general, often unorganised, sentiment among the people
Public opinion can only be expressed through political parties
Pressure groups never attempt to influence government policy
Public opinion is always more organised than any pressure group
questions.explanation: While both can shape government decisions, pressure groups are structured, organised bodies with specific goals, whereas public opinion is a broader, more diffuse expression of popular sentiment.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The Civil Service refers to the
options: military and police personnel
judges serving in the judiciary
body of permanent, non-political officials who implement government policies
elected members of the legislature
questions.explanation: The Civil Service consists of professional, typically non-partisan administrators who provide continuity in government by implementing policy regardless of which political party is in power.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A key characteristic of an ideal civil service is
options: the right to make laws independently of the legislature
complete independence from any form of government oversight
active membership in a specific political party
political neutrality, allowing it to serve any government of the day impartially
questions.explanation: Civil servants are expected to remain politically neutral, faithfully implementing the policies of whichever government is in power, rather than favouring a particular political party.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of the following is a common problem facing the civil service in many developing countries?
options: Too few civil servants relative to the population's needs everywhere
Complete absence of any hierarchical structure
Excessive political neutrality that never causes any issues
Bureaucratic bottlenecks, corruption, and inefficiency
questions.explanation: Civil services in many developing countries often struggle with slow, overly bureaucratic processes, corruption, and general inefficiency, undermining effective public service delivery.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A public corporation is established mainly to
options: serve as a branch of a specific political party
provide essential goods or services to the public, often in sectors considered too important for purely private control
replace the judiciary in resolving legal disputes
generate maximum profit for private shareholders
questions.explanation: Public corporations are government-owned entities set up to deliver key public services (like electricity or transportation), often prioritising public welfare over pure profit maximisation.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Local government, as the third tier of government in Nigeria, is primarily responsible for
options: commanding the national armed forces
making laws for the entire federation
conducting the country's foreign relations
administering affairs at the grassroots level closest to the people
questions.explanation: Local government exists as the tier of administration closest to ordinary citizens, handling grassroots issues such as local infrastructure, markets, and primary healthcare.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of the following is a common source of revenue for local governments in Nigeria?
options: Direct taxation of foreign embassies
Direct control over national customs duties
Revenue from international trade agreements
Statutory allocation from the federation account
questions.explanation: Local governments in Nigeria primarily rely on statutory allocations from the federation account, along with locally generated revenue such as rates and levies, to fund their operations.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of the following is a common problem facing local government administration in Nigeria?
options: Complete financial and administrative independence from the states
Too much direct citizen participation in decision-making
An overabundance of skilled administrative personnel
Inadequate funding and excessive control by state governments
questions.explanation: Nigerian local governments often struggle with insufficient funding and significant interference or control from state governments, limiting their autonomy and effectiveness.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The pre-colonial Hausa-Fulani political system was primarily organised around
options: a decentralised system with no recognisable central authority
rule by an assembly of age-grade groups only
a purely democratic system with universal adult suffrage
a centralised emirate system headed by an Emir, supported by appointed officials
questions.explanation: The Hausa-Fulani political system was highly centralised, with an Emir at the apex, supported by a hierarchy of appointed officials (such as the Waziri and district heads) administering the emirate.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: In the pre-colonial Hausa-Fulani system, the Emir was assisted in administration by an official known as the
options: Oba
Waziri (Vizier)
Obi
Eze
questions.explanation: The Waziri served as a chief adviser and administrator to the Emir, playing a role somewhat similar to a modern-day prime minister within the emirate system.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The pre-colonial Yoruba political system was traditionally headed by a
options: purely elected village council with no traditional ruler
single military dictator with no legitimacy
religious leader with no political authority
monarch known as the Oba, supported by chiefs and councils
questions.explanation: The traditional Yoruba political system was monarchical, headed by an Oba, but tempered by councils of chiefs (such as the Oyomesi in the Oyo Empire) who provided checks on his authority.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: In pre-colonial Yoruba political systems, the council of kingmakers and chiefs known as the Oyomesi served mainly to
options: act purely as a religious body with no political function
have no influence at all over the Alaafin's decisions
check the power of the Alaafin and could, in extreme cases, demand his removal
replace the Alaafin as the sole ruler of the kingdom
questions.explanation: The Oyomesi acted as a check on the Alaafin of Oyo's power, and under extreme circumstances, could even present him with an empty calabash as a demand that he take his own life, effectively removing him from power.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The pre-colonial Igbo political system is generally described as
options: identical in structure to the Yoruba Oba system
a decentralised, republican system without a single centralised traditional ruler
a system ruled entirely by a single hereditary emperor
a highly centralised monarchy similar to the Hausa-Fulani emirate system
questions.explanation: Unlike the centralised Hausa-Fulani and Yoruba systems, the traditional Igbo political system was largely acephalous (without a single head), relying instead on councils of elders, age-grades, and title societies for governance.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: In the pre-colonial Igbo political system, decision-making was often carried out through
options: an emir supported by appointed district heads
a foreign-appointed colonial governor
village assemblies, councils of elders, and age-grade associations
a single all-powerful hereditary king
questions.explanation: Igbo communities typically governed themselves through participatory structures such as village general assemblies, councils of elders, and age-grade groups, reflecting a more decentralised, consensus-driven approach to authority.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Title societies, such as the Ozo title in Igbo land, functioned mainly to
options: confer social status and political influence upon those who attained the title
replace the need for any council of elders
serve as the sole military command structure
represent a purely ceremonial role with no social significance
questions.explanation: Title societies granted successful members enhanced social prestige and often a voice in community decision-making, forming an important part of the decentralised Igbo governance structure.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A key difference between the pre-colonial Hausa-Fulani and Igbo political systems was that the Hausa-Fulani system was
options: controlled by colonial administrators from the outset
centralised under an Emir, while the Igbo system was largely decentralised
entirely without any traditional leadership structure, unlike the Igbo system
based on universal adult suffrage, unlike the Igbo system
questions.explanation: This distinction is a classic feature of Nigerian pre-colonial political history: the Hausa-Fulani's strongly centralised emirate structure versus the Igbo's more decentralised, republican-style governance.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The policy of Indirect Rule, adopted by the British in colonial Nigeria, involved
options: immediate grant of full self-government to Nigerians
direct rule by British officials with no involvement of traditional authorities
governing through existing traditional rulers and institutions, under overall British supervision
the complete abolition of all traditional rulers and institutions
questions.explanation: Indirect Rule, associated with Lord Lugard, used existing traditional political structures (like Emirs) as intermediaries to administer colonial policy, reducing the number of British officials needed.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Indirect Rule was most successfully implemented in colonial Nigeria in the
options: Western Region only, due to a complete absence of traditional rulers
entire country equally, with no regional variation in success
Eastern Region, due to its decentralised political structures
Northern Region, due to the existing centralised emirate system
questions.explanation: The North's centralised Hausa-Fulani emirate system, with clear hierarchical authority, was well suited to Indirect Rule, whereas the decentralised Igbo system in the East made it more difficult to implement effectively.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A major challenge to implementing Indirect Rule in Eastern Nigeria was that the
options: region had no population large enough to govern
decentralised Igbo political system lacked the centralised traditional rulers the policy relied upon
British had no colonial interest in the Eastern Region at all
Igbo people had no interest in trade with the British
questions.explanation: Since Indirect Rule depended on existing centralised traditional authority, the British faced difficulties in the East, sometimes resorting to appointing 'Warrant Chiefs' who lacked genuine traditional legitimacy.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The Clifford Constitution of 1922 is significant mainly for
options: granting Nigeria full independence from British rule
establishing a fully federal system of government for Nigeria
abolishing all forms of legislative council in Nigeria
introducing the elective principle, allowing a limited number of Nigerians to be elected into the Legislative Council
questions.explanation: The 1922 Clifford Constitution was notable for introducing limited elections, allowing a small number of Nigerians (in Lagos and Calabar) to be elected to the Legislative Council for the first time.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The Richards Constitution of 1946 is significant mainly for
options: introducing universal adult suffrage across Nigeria
abolishing the position of Governor-General
introducing regionalism by dividing Nigeria into three regions (North, East, West)
granting Nigeria complete independence
questions.explanation: The Richards Constitution laid the foundation for Nigerian federalism by dividing the country into three regions, each with its own regional legislative assembly.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The Macpherson Constitution of 1951 is significant mainly for
options: abolishing the regional structure created by the Richards Constitution
establishing Nigeria's first military government
granting Nigeria full independence from Britain
introducing a greater degree of Nigerian participation in central government and expanding the elective principle
questions.explanation: The Macpherson Constitution expanded Nigerian involvement in governance at the centre and further developed representative institutions, though it also revealed growing regional tensions.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The Lyttelton Constitution of 1954 is significant mainly for
options: formally establishing Nigeria as a federation with defined powers for the regions and the centre
establishing a unitary, rather than federal, system of government
abolishing the office of Regional Premier
granting Nigeria immediate independence
questions.explanation: The 1954 Lyttelton Constitution firmly established Nigeria's federal structure, clearly defining the division of powers between the regional governments and the central government.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Nationalist movements in colonial Nigeria emerged mainly in response to
options: a request from the British government for Nigerians to seek independence
the total absence of any educated Nigerian elite
a lack of any economic or political grievances under colonial rule
dissatisfaction with colonial rule and a desire for self-governance and independence
questions.explanation: Nationalist movements, led by figures like Herbert Macaulay, Nnamdi Azikiwe, and Obafemi Awolowo, arose from growing Nigerian dissatisfaction with colonial domination and a push for self-rule.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The National Council of Nigeria and the Cameroons (NCNC) was significant as an early Nigerian
options: purely religious organisation with no political goals
colonial administrative body established by the British
military faction opposing civilian rule
nationalist political organisation advocating for self-government
questions.explanation: The NCNC, led notably by Herbert Macaulay and later Nnamdi Azikiwe, was one of Nigeria's earliest and most prominent nationalist political parties advocating for self-determination.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of the following best describes the general impact of British colonial rule on Nigeria's political development?
options: It immediately granted Nigeria a fully independent, self-sufficient government
It had no effect whatsoever on Nigeria's traditional political systems
It completely eliminated regional and ethnic distinctions within Nigeria
It introduced Western political and administrative structures while altering pre-existing indigenous systems of governance
questions.explanation: Colonial rule fundamentally reshaped Nigeria's political landscape by introducing Western-style institutions and constitutional frameworks, while significantly altering (and in some cases undermining) existing indigenous governance systems.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The 1960 Independence Constitution established Nigeria as a
options: federation with a parliamentary system of government under a constitutional monarch
unitary state under an executive president
one-party socialist state
military-controlled federation
questions.explanation: At independence in 1960, Nigeria adopted a parliamentary system, retaining the British monarch as ceremonial Head of State, represented locally by a Governor-General.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The 1963 Republican Constitution is significant mainly because it
options: abolished the federal structure of Nigeria
granted Nigeria independence from British rule
made Nigeria a republic, replacing the British monarch with a Nigerian President as Head of State
introduced military rule for the first time
questions.explanation: The 1963 Constitution transformed Nigeria into a full republic, replacing the British monarch as Head of State with an indigenous Nigerian President, while retaining the parliamentary system.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The 1979 Constitution introduced which significant change to Nigeria's system of government?
options: A one-party socialist system of government
A presidential system of government, replacing the parliamentary system
The abolition of the federal structure
A return to colonial-style Indirect Rule
questions.explanation: The 1979 Constitution marked Nigeria's shift from the parliamentary system inherited at independence to a presidential system modelled substantially on that of the United States.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The 1999 Constitution, under which Nigeria currently operates, established a
options: parliamentary system of government under a ceremonial monarch
presidential system of government with a federal structure
purely unitary system of government
one-party state with no multi-party competition
questions.explanation: The 1999 Constitution (as amended) continues to govern Nigeria today, maintaining a federal, presidential system of government with three tiers: federal, state, and local government.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of the following is a key feature common to Nigeria's post-independence constitutions (1963, 1979, 1999)?
options: Rule exclusively by unelected traditional rulers
The complete absence of a written constitution
A federal system of government dividing power between the centre and constituent units
A single, unitary structure with no regional or state divisions
questions.explanation: Despite differences in the form of executive government (parliamentary vs. presidential), Nigeria's constitutions since independence have consistently maintained a federal structure.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The transition from a parliamentary to a presidential system of government in Nigeria was formalised by the
options: 1960 Independence Constitution
Richards Constitution of 1946
1979 Constitution
1963 Republican Constitution
questions.explanation: While the 1960 and 1963 constitutions retained a parliamentary framework, it was the 1979 Constitution that introduced the presidential system Nigeria has retained (with interruptions) since.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Under the 1999 Constitution, the President of Nigeria serves as both
options: only Head of Government, with a separate ceremonial Head of State
Head of State and Head of Government
only a ceremonial Head of State with no executive powers
a purely symbolic figure with no constitutional role
questions.explanation: Under Nigeria's presidential system, the President combines the roles of Head of State (ceremonial representative of the nation) and Head of Government (in charge of the executive branch), unlike the separated roles in a parliamentary system.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which post-independence Nigerian constitution first introduced the Federal Character Principle to ensure fair representation of Nigeria's diverse groups in government?
options: The 1979 Constitution
The 1963 Republican Constitution
The Lyttelton Constitution of 1954
The 1960 Independence Constitution
questions.explanation: The Federal Character Principle, aimed at ensuring no particular ethnic or sectional group dominates public appointments, was formally introduced under the 1979 Constitution.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A major cause of military intervention in Nigerian politics historically has been
options: unanimous public satisfaction with civilian rule
widespread political instability, corruption, and electoral malpractice under civilian governments
a complete absence of any political parties
excessive stability and efficiency of civilian government
questions.explanation: Military coups in Nigeria's history were frequently justified by the military as necessary responses to perceived political instability, corruption, and failures of the preceding civilian administrations.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Under military rule in Nigeria, governmental power was typically concentrated in a body known as the
options: Council of State comprised only of civilians
Federal Executive Council elected by the people
National Assembly
Supreme Military Council (or similar ruling council)
questions.explanation: Military regimes in Nigeria generally centralised power in a small ruling council of top military officers (variously named, such as the Supreme Military Council or Provisional Ruling Council), which issued decrees with the force of law.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: During military rule, laws were typically enacted through
options: decisions made solely by the judiciary
referenda conducted among the general public
decrees issued by the ruling military council, rather than through a legislature
debate and voting within an elected National Assembly
questions.explanation: Since military governments typically suspended or dissolved the legislature, laws were instead promulgated as decrees by the ruling military authority, bypassing normal legislative processes.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: One commonly cited achievement of military regimes in Nigeria has been
options: increased citizen participation in lawmaking
the strengthening of multi-party democratic institutions
the permanent elimination of political corruption
swift decision-making unburdened by lengthy legislative debate, particularly during national emergencies
questions.explanation: Supporters of military rule sometimes point to its capacity for rapid, centralised decision-making, useful during crises, though this often came at the cost of democratic checks and civil liberties.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A commonly cited weakness of military rule in Nigeria has been
options: the suppression of fundamental human rights and lack of accountability to the electorate
too much power vested in an elected legislature
excessive checks and balances slowing down governance
overly transparent and participatory decision-making processes
questions.explanation: Military regimes were frequently criticised for curtailing civil liberties, operating without the accountability mechanisms of elections, and concentrating power without meaningful checks.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The transition from military to civilian rule in Nigeria typically involved
options: drafting a new or amended constitution and conducting elections to usher in a democratically elected government
the immediate abolition of the federal system of government
the permanent retention of power by the military
rule being handed directly to a foreign government
questions.explanation: Transitions from military to civilian rule in Nigeria's history generally followed a process of constitutional reform and organised elections to restore a democratically elected government.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Nigeria's foreign policy refers to the
options: policies exclusively concerning Nigeria's military structure at home
internal policies governing Nigeria's domestic economy alone
laws governing trade solely within Nigeria's borders
strategies and principles guiding Nigeria's relations with other countries and international bodies
questions.explanation: Foreign policy encompasses the principles and strategies a country adopts in conducting its relations, diplomacy, and interactions with other states and international organisations.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of the following is a core principle guiding Nigeria's foreign policy since independence?
options: Total avoidance of any international organisation membership
Exclusive alliance with a single foreign superpower
Complete isolation from all other African countries
Africa as the centrepiece of Nigeria's foreign policy
questions.explanation: Nigeria has consistently emphasised the promotion of African unity, decolonisation, and development as the central focus (the 'centrepiece') of its foreign policy since gaining independence.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of the following is a major determinant of a country's foreign policy?
options: The personal hobbies of individual government ministers
The country's economic resources and strategic national interests
The colour of the country's national flag
The number of public holidays celebrated annually
questions.explanation: Foreign policy decisions are typically shaped by tangible factors such as a nation's economic strength, security concerns, historical ties, and overall strategic national interests.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Nigeria played a significant leadership role in supporting the independence and anti-apartheid struggles of which Southern African country?
options: Egypt
South Africa
Kenya
Morocco
questions.explanation: Nigeria was a vocal and active supporter of the anti-apartheid movement in South Africa, providing diplomatic, financial, and moral support to end apartheid rule.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Nigeria's relations with world powers, such as the United States and the United Kingdom, are generally guided by considerations of
options: unconditional agreement with all their foreign policy positions
total isolation from any political or economic engagement
abandonment of any independent Nigerian foreign policy stance
mutual economic benefit, diplomatic cooperation, and international security
questions.explanation: Nigeria's relations with major world powers are typically shaped by pragmatic considerations of trade, investment, diplomatic partnership, and shared security interests, while still asserting independent policy positions.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Nigeria's foreign policy towards other African states has generally emphasised
options: the annexation of neighbouring territories
support only for countries that share Nigeria's exact system of government
complete non-involvement in regional African affairs
Pan-Africanism and support for regional cooperation and integration
questions.explanation: Nigeria has generally championed Pan-African ideals, supporting regional cooperation, peacekeeping, and integration efforts across the African continent, consistent with its 'Africa as centrepiece' policy.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The United Nations Organization (UNO) was established mainly to
options: regulate the internal domestic policies of member states directly
serve as a single world government replacing individual nations
function exclusively as a global trading company
promote international peace, security, and cooperation among nations
questions.explanation: The UN was founded after World War II with the primary aim of maintaining international peace and security while fostering cooperation on economic, social, and humanitarian issues among member states.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which organ of the United Nations is primarily responsible for maintaining international peace and security?
options: The Security Council
The General Assembly
The International Court of Justice
The Economic and Social Council
questions.explanation: The UN Security Council holds primary responsibility for addressing threats to international peace and security, including the authority to authorise peacekeeping missions and sanctions.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The permanent members of the United Nations Security Council, each holding veto power, are
options: Nigeria, South Africa, Egypt, Kenya, and Ghana
Germany, Japan, India, Brazil, and Canada
all 193 member states of the United Nations equally
the United States, United Kingdom, France, Russia, and China
questions.explanation: The UN Security Council has five permanent members with veto power (the US, UK, France, Russia, and China), alongside ten non-permanent members elected for two-year terms.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The Commonwealth of Nations is an international organisation whose members are mainly
options: countries that were formerly part of the British Empire
countries that have never had any historical ties to Britain
restricted only to countries in the Americas
exclusively countries located in Europe
questions.explanation: The Commonwealth is a voluntary association of predominantly former British colonies and territories, including Nigeria, that cooperate on shared values like democracy and development.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The African Union (AU) was established mainly to promote
options: competition and conflict among African nations
the re-establishment of colonial rule in Africa
unity, cooperation, and development among African states
the political and economic isolation of African states from the rest of the world
questions.explanation: The AU (successor to the Organisation of African Unity) works to promote political and economic integration, peace, security, and development across the African continent.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) was established mainly to promote
options: military conflict among West African states
trade exclusively between West Africa and Europe
economic integration and cooperation among West African countries
the political isolation of Nigeria from its neighbours
questions.explanation: ECOWAS aims to foster economic cooperation, free movement of goods and people, and regional integration among its West African member states, including Nigeria.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Nigeria has historically played a significant peacekeeping role within ECOWAS, notably through its leadership contributions to the ECOWAS Monitoring Group known as
options: AU Peace and Security Council
NATO
ECOMOG
UN Security Council
questions.explanation: ECOMOG (ECOWAS Monitoring Group) was a peacekeeping force established by ECOWAS, in which Nigeria played a leading and prominent role, notably during conflicts in Liberia and Sierra Leone.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: International organisations such as the UN, Commonwealth, AU, and ECOWAS generally benefit member countries mainly by
options: eliminating the sovereignty of all member states entirely
guaranteeing unlimited financial wealth to every member state
forcing all member states to adopt an identical system of government
providing platforms for cooperation, conflict resolution, and collective action on shared challenges
questions.explanation: These organisations create structured forums where member states can collaborate on common political, economic, security, and social challenges, while generally still respecting national sovereignty.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Nigeria's membership in international organisations like the UN and AU reflects its foreign policy commitment to
options: multilateral cooperation and collective diplomacy on the world stage
withdrawal from all forms of international engagement
unilateral action without regard for international consensus
complete political isolation from other nations
questions.explanation: Nigeria's active participation in these international bodies demonstrates its foreign policy preference for engaging diplomatically and cooperatively with the wider international community, rather than pursuing isolation.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of the following best describes the role of the United Nations General Assembly?
options: An organisation limited only to economic issues in Europe
A body with the exclusive power to authorise military action against any nation
A court that settles legal disputes between individual citizens
A forum where all member states have equal representation to discuss and vote on a wide range of international issues
questions.explanation: The General Assembly is the main deliberative body of the UN, where every member state, regardless of size or power, has equal voting rights on a broad range of global issues.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The International Court of Justice (ICJ), the principal judicial organ of the United Nations, is primarily responsible for
options: settling legal disputes between states and providing advisory opinions on international legal questions
administering humanitarian aid directly to refugees
managing the UN's annual budget and finances
enforcing UN Security Council resolutions with military force
questions.explanation: The ICJ, based in The Hague, adjudicates legal disputes submitted by states and offers advisory opinions on international legal matters referred to it by authorised UN bodies.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Max Weber distinguished three types of legitimate authority. Which pairing correctly matches a type with its basis?
options: Traditional authority — rests on a written constitution ratified by referendum
Charismatic authority — rests on impersonal rules enacted through proper legal procedure
Legal-rational authority — rests on the exceptional heroism or personal qualities of a leader
Traditional authority — rests on established belief in the sanctity of long-standing customs
questions.explanation: Weber classified traditional authority as deriving legitimacy from long-established customs and hereditary status, unlike charismatic (personal qualities) or legal-rational (codified rules) authority.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A government may possess effective power over its territory yet still be widely regarded as illegitimate. This scenario best illustrates that
options: power and legitimacy are identical concepts and cannot diverge
power is the capacity to compel obedience while legitimacy is the popular acceptance of the right to rule, and one can exist without the other
sovereignty automatically confers legitimacy on any government
legitimacy is solely determined by international recognition
questions.explanation: Power is the ability to enforce compliance, whereas legitimacy is the moral and psychological acceptance of authority by the governed; a regime can hold power without being seen as legitimate.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Internal sovereignty is best distinguished from external sovereignty in that internal sovereignty refers to
options: recognition by other independent states in the international community
the state's capacity to wage war against other nations
membership of regional organisations such as the African Union
supreme, final authority over persons and affairs within the state's own territory
questions.explanation: Internal sovereignty is the supreme authority a state exercises over all persons, groups and institutions within its borders, while external sovereignty concerns independence from outside control and recognition by other states.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Political socialization is best defined as the process by which
options: a state acquires new territory through conquest
individuals acquire political values, attitudes and knowledge that shape their orientation to the political system
political parties select candidates for elective office
a government transfers power to a successor administration
questions.explanation: Political socialization describes the lifelong process, occurring through agents such as family, school and media, by which individuals internalise the political values and norms of their society.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Political culture, as used by political scientists, refers primarily to
options: the formal legal framework establishing a country's arms of government
the artistic and literary output of a nation's citizens
the pattern of individual orientations — cognitive, affective and evaluative — towards the political system shared within a society
the census data used to apportion legislative seats
questions.explanation: Political culture concerns the shared beliefs, values and attitudes citizens hold about their political system, distinct from the formal institutional or legal structure of government.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of the following best explains why a State is considered logically prior to, and more permanent than, any particular government?
options: A State can exist only where a single political party is in office
A State ceases to exist whenever its government is overthrown
A government is merely the machinery through which state sovereignty is exercised at a given time, and it may change while the State persists
Government and State are interchangeable terms with no meaningful distinction
questions.explanation: The State is a permanent political community, while government is the temporary body of persons and institutions exercising state authority, which can change through elections or coups without the State itself dissolving.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A stateless society, as anthropologists use the term in describing some pre-colonial African communities, is one in which
options: political authority is diffused among kinship groups, age-grades or lineage councils rather than concentrated in a centralised ruler
there is no organised political authority whatsoever and total anarchy prevails
a written constitution formally abolishes the office of chief
sovereignty is vested exclusively in a colonial governor
questions.explanation: Stateless societies, such as the pre-colonial Igbo, lacked a centralised monarchical authority but were not anarchic; governance was exercised through decentralised kinship, age-grade and lineage institutions.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which distinction correctly separates 'power' from 'influence' in political analysis?
options: Influence is exercised only by courts while power is exercised only by legislatures
Influence always requires a constitutional office while power does not
Power and influence are synonyms used interchangeably in political science
Power involves the ability to compel compliance often backed by sanctions, while influence involves shaping decisions through persuasion without coercive sanction
questions.explanation: Power typically carries the capacity to enforce obedience through sanctions, whereas influence achieves compliance through persuasion, bargaining or moral suasion without formal coercive backing.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: In distinguishing an oligarchy from an aristocracy, the key criterion political scientists apply is that
options: an oligarchy is rule by the wealthy few for their own selfish interest, while an aristocracy is rule by a privileged few claiming superior merit or birth
an aristocracy always involves rule by military officers while an oligarchy never does
an oligarchy is a democratic system while an aristocracy is not
there is no meaningful difference; both terms describe identical systems
questions.explanation: Aristocracy denotes rule by a supposedly superior minority (often based on birth or merit) claiming to govern in the common good, whereas oligarchy denotes rule by a small elite, typically the wealthy, primarily serving its own interests.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of the following best captures the essential difference between a federal and a confederal system of government?
options: Federal systems cannot have a bicameral legislature while confederations must
A federation has no written constitution while a confederation always does
A confederation has a stronger central government than a federation

In a federation, sovereignty is divided constitutionally between central and component governments each acting directly on citizens, whereas in a confederation sovereignty resides with the constituent states which retain the right to secede
questions.explanation: Federalism creates a constitutionally entrenched division of power in which both levels act directly on citizens, while a confederation is a looser alliance of sovereign states retaining ultimate authority, including the right of withdrawal.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A defining structural feature that distinguishes a presidential system from a parliamentary system is that in a presidential system
options: the executive is drawn from and remains accountable to the legislature through votes of no confidence
the head of state and head of government are fused in one office that is separately elected and not accountable to the legislature for its continuation in office
the legislature can be dissolved at will by the prime minister
cabinet ministers must simultaneously be sitting members of parliament
questions.explanation: In presidential systems, the president is separately elected for a fixed term and does not depend on continued legislative confidence, unlike a parliamentary system where the executive emerges from and can be dismissed by the legislature.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A rigid constitution is best described as one in which
options: amendment can be achieved through a simple majority vote in an ordinary legislative session
amendment requires a special procedure more demanding than that for ordinary legislation, such as a supermajority or referendum
the constitution is entirely unwritten and based on convention
the constitution cannot be amended under any circumstances whatsoever
questions.explanation: Rigidity refers to the presence of special, more demanding amendment procedures, not to the impossibility of amendment; Nigeria's 1999 Constitution, for example, requires two-thirds and state assembly approval.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which statement correctly distinguishes an unwritten constitution from a written one, using the United Kingdom and the United States as examples?
options: Both the UK and US constitutions are codified in a single authoritative document
The UK has no constitution at all, while the US Constitution is entirely oral tradition
The UK's constitution is uncodified, deriving from statutes, conventions, and judicial precedent, while the US Constitution is a single codified document
An unwritten constitution cannot be amended, while a written one can always be amended by simple majority
questions.explanation: Britain's constitution is described as unwritten because it is uncodified, drawing on multiple sources including statute, common law and convention, whereas the United States has a single codified written document.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Direct democracy differs from representative (indirect) democracy chiefly in that direct democracy
options: can only occur in states with a population above one hundred million
involves citizens making political decisions themselves, such as through referenda or plebiscites, rather than through elected representatives
requires the existence of at least three political parties
eliminates the need for any form of citizenship
questions.explanation: Direct democracy allows citizens to participate personally in decision-making, for example through referenda, while representative democracy delegates decision-making to elected officials.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of the following is the most accurate distinction between a republic and a monarchy?
options: A republic has no executive branch of government
A republic must always be a federation while a monarchy must always be unitary
A monarchy cannot have a written constitution
A republic's head of state derives office through some form of election or appointment rather than heredity, while a monarchy's head of state typically succeeds by hereditary right
questions.explanation: The defining feature of a republic is a non-hereditary head of state, usually chosen through election, in contrast to a monarchy where succession is typically hereditary.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A theocracy is a system of government in which
options: supreme authority rests with the military high command
the civil service exercises ultimate sovereign authority
power rotates strictly among elected regional governors
governance is conducted according to religious law with rulers claiming divine sanction or acting as agents of a deity
questions.explanation: In a theocracy, political authority is exercised in accordance with religious doctrine, with rulers deriving their legitimacy from claimed divine authority rather than popular mandate or secular law.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of the following is a genuine check the legislature holds over the executive under a presidential system such as Nigeria's, rather than over the judiciary?
options: The power to grant the prerogative of mercy to convicted persons
The power to issue binding judicial precedents
The power to try civil and criminal cases at first instance
The power to confirm ministerial and other key executive appointments and to override a presidential veto by a qualified majority
questions.explanation: Legislatures typically check the executive by confirming key appointments and by having the capacity to override an executive veto with a supermajority, distinguishing this from judicial functions.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The principle of judicial independence is best undermined by which of the following?
options: Executive control over the appointment, discipline, and removal of judges without meaningful checks
Payment of judicial salaries from a Consolidated Revenue Fund not subject to annual legislative vote
Security of tenure for judges guaranteed until a fixed retirement age
A constitutional bar on judges holding other paid employment while in office
questions.explanation: Judicial independence is compromised when the executive can unilaterally appoint, discipline or remove judges, since this creates dependence and potential for political interference in adjudication.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Judicial activism, as opposed to judicial restraint, describes a tendency for courts to
options: strictly defer to the literal wording of statutes and avoid overturning legislative or executive decisions
delegate all interpretive authority to the legislature
refuse to hear any case involving constitutional interpretation
interpret the constitution broadly and be willing to overturn legislative or executive actions to advance perceived justice or evolving social values
questions.explanation: Judicial activism describes courts taking an expansive interpretive approach and readily striking down or reshaping legislative and executive action, in contrast to judicial restraint's deference to elected branches.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The doctrine of separation of powers, as articulated by Montesquieu, is most accurately summarised as
options: a single body should exercise legislative, executive and judicial functions to ensure efficiency
only the legislature should exist, with executive and judicial functions abolished
legislative, executive and judicial powers should be vested in separate organs and personnel, primarily to prevent the concentration and abuse of power
the executive should have absolute power to override both the legislature and judiciary at will
questions.explanation: Montesquieu argued that liberty is best safeguarded when legislative, executive and judicial powers are held by distinct organs and personnel, preventing any one branch from becoming tyrannical.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: In strict theory, a pure application of separation of powers would be inconsistent with which practice found in Nigeria's presidential system?
options: The President nominating ministers who must then be screened and confirmed by the Senate
The National Assembly having exclusive power to make laws on matters in the Exclusive Legislative List
The judiciary having sole responsibility for interpreting the constitution
The President being constitutionally barred from serving more than two terms
questions.explanation: Requiring Senate confirmation of ministerial nominees blends legislative involvement into an executive appointment function, illustrating checks and balances rather than a strict, watertight separation of powers.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The primary rationale for bicameralism in a federal state such as Nigeria is that
options: it slows down the legislative process unnecessarily and serves no other purpose
a second chamber, often representing constituent states equally, provides a check on the popularly apportioned lower house and safeguards federal interests
it eliminates the need for an executive veto
it allows the judiciary to bypass legislative approval for new laws
questions.explanation: A bicameral legislature in federations typically pairs a population-based lower house with an upper house giving equal or special representation to constituent units, protecting federalism and providing additional scrutiny.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Delegated legislation, whereby the executive makes detailed rules under authority granted by an enabling Act of the legislature, is primarily justified on the grounds that
options: it allows the executive to bypass judicial review entirely
the legislature lacks the technical expertise and time to formulate every detailed regulation, so it delegates rule-making within limits it sets
it transfers full law-making sovereignty permanently to the executive
it is required by the doctrine of separation of powers
questions.explanation: Delegated legislation exists because legislatures often lack the specialised expertise and time to draft technical regulations, so they authorise the executive to fill in details within a framework the legislature has set.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of the following best distinguishes the 'original jurisdiction' of a court from its 'appellate jurisdiction'?
options: Original jurisdiction applies only to criminal matters while appellate jurisdiction applies only to civil matters
Original jurisdiction is the authority to hear a case for the first time, while appellate jurisdiction is the authority to review decisions already made by a lower court
Appellate jurisdiction is exercised exclusively by magistrate courts
Original jurisdiction and appellate jurisdiction are identical in meaning
questions.explanation: Original jurisdiction refers to a court's power to hear and determine a case in the first instance, whereas appellate jurisdiction is the power to review and revise decisions rendered by a lower court.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of the following most accurately distinguishes scientific socialism (Marxism) from utopian socialism?
options: Scientific socialism, as developed by Marx and Engels, claims to base the inevitability of socialist transformation on a materialist analysis of historical class struggle, whereas utopian socialism relies on moral appeals and idealistic model communities without such a systematic theory
Utopian socialism advocates violent revolution while scientific socialism rejects revolution entirely
Scientific socialism supports private ownership of the means of production while utopian socialism opposes it
There is no meaningful theoretical distinction between the two forms of socialism
questions.explanation: Marx and Engels distinguished their 'scientific socialism', grounded in historical materialism and class analysis, from earlier utopian socialists who relied on moral persuasion and idealised experimental communities.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Fascism and Nazism both emphasise extreme nationalism and a single-party dictatorship, but Nazism is additionally distinguished by
options: its advocacy of a stateless, classless society
its rejection of the concept of a nation-state entirely
its explicit doctrine of racial superiority and antisemitism as central to state ideology
its promotion of internationalist working-class solidarity across borders
questions.explanation: While both ideologies are ultranationalist and authoritarian, Nazism uniquely centred an explicit doctrine of Aryan racial superiority and antisemitic persecution as core state policy.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Under feudalism as a politico-economic system, political power and land tenure were organised primarily around
options: a free market in which land was bought and sold without restriction by anyone
state ownership of all land with equal distribution to every citizen
universal adult suffrage determining land allocation
a contractual hierarchy of lords and vassals in which land (the fief) was granted in exchange for military service and loyalty
questions.explanation: Feudalism was structured around a hierarchical bond in which vassals held land (fiefs) granted by lords in return for military service, labour and loyalty, rather than market exchange or state redistribution.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Communalism, as practised in many pre-colonial African societies, is best characterised by
options: private, individual ownership of land as an absolute and exclusive right
state ownership of all means of production under a single ruling party
collective or communal ownership of land and resources by the kinship group or community, with the individual holding usufructuary rights
a rigid class system based on inherited nobility titles
questions.explanation: Communalism vested ultimate ownership of land in the community or kinship group, with individuals enjoying rights of use rather than absolute private ownership, reflecting communal rather than individualist or state control.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A key ideological distinction between classical liberal capitalism and communism concerns
options: capitalism advocates private ownership of the means of production and a market-driven economy, while communism advocates collective ownership of the means of production and the eventual abolition of class and the state
capitalism requires a one-party state while communism requires a multi-party state
communism promotes private property rights above all else
capitalism and communism are simply different names for the same economic system
questions.explanation: Capitalism rests on private ownership and market allocation of resources, whereas communism envisions collective ownership of production and, ultimately, a classless, stateless society.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which statement best explains why communism is often described as the theoretical end-stage envisioned by Marxist socialism, rather than a synonym for it?
options: Communism refers only to religious organisation while socialism refers only to economic organisation
Communism precedes socialism chronologically in Marxist theory
Socialism and communism describe identical political-economic arrangements with no stages involved

Marxist theory treats socialism as a transitional stage of proletarian dictatorship redistributing ownership, while communism denotes the ultimate classless, stateless society that socialism is meant to produce
