questions.explanation: In orthodox Marxist theory, socialism is a transitional phase in which the proletariat controls the state to eliminate class distinctions, ultimately giving way to communism, a stateless and classless society.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of the following is the most important function a constitution performs in a modern state?
options: It establishes the structure, powers and limits of government organs and defines the relationship between the state and citizens
It merely records the history of the ruling political party
It replaces the need for any legislature to make laws
It serves only a ceremonial function with no binding legal effect
questions.explanation: A constitution's core function is to establish government structures, allocate and limit powers among organs of state, and define citizens' rights and obligations vis-à-vis the state.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Constitutional conventions, as a source of constitutional rules in systems like the United Kingdom, are best described as
options: established, non-legal customary practices that are generally observed by political actors though not directly enforceable by the courts
binding statutes passed by the legislature and enforceable directly in ordinary courts
judicial precedents that override statutory law
provisions found exclusively in a country's written, codified constitution
questions.explanation: Constitutional conventions are unwritten customary practices that political actors follow out of a sense of constitutional obligation, but which, unlike statutes, are not directly enforceable in a court of law.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A written constitution is generally considered advantageous over an unwritten one mainly because it
options: is always easier to change than an unwritten constitution
can never be amended once adopted
eliminates the possibility of any constitutional crisis
provides clarity, certainty and a definite reference point for resolving disputes about governmental powers
questions.explanation: Codification in a single authoritative document gives a written constitution clarity and certainty as a definite reference for settling disputes over the distribution and limits of governmental power.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which scenario best illustrates a constitutional crisis arising from an ambiguity in constitutional provisions rather than an outright breach of law?
options: A president dissolving the legislature in clear violation of an explicit constitutional prohibition
A court delivering a judgment strictly consistent with settled constitutional text
A legislature passing a routine annual budget as required by the constitution
Rival interpretations emerging over who should act as head of state when the constitution's succession provisions are unclear following a sudden vacancy
questions.explanation: A constitutional crisis of ambiguity typically arises when a genuine dispute exists over how unclear or silent provisions should be interpreted, such as succession arrangements, rather than a straightforward violation of explicit rules.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Autochthony, as applied to a constitution, refers to the quality of a constitution being
options: imposed entirely by a foreign colonial power without local input
applicable only to monarchies
unwritten and based purely on oral tradition
home-grown, deriving its legal validity from the will of the indigenous people rather than from an external authority such as a colonial parliament
questions.explanation: An autochthonous constitution is one that derives its authority and legitimacy from the indigenous population itself, rather than being granted or imposed by an external colonial power, a concern in Nigeria's 1963 Republican Constitution.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A key distinction between citizenship acquired by 'registration' and citizenship acquired by 'naturalisation' under Nigerian law is that
options: naturalisation applies only to children born in Nigeria to Nigerian parents

registration is generally available to certain categories such as foreign spouses of citizens or persons of Nigerian descent after satisfying set conditions, while naturalisation is a more general process open to qualifying foreigners typically requiring longer residence and presidential discretion
registration is granted automatically to every foreign resident regardless of any conditions
there is no procedural difference; both terms describe an identical legal process
questions.explanation: Under Nigerian nationality law, registration is a somewhat easier route for specified categories like foreign spouses, while naturalisation is a more general, discretionary process for other qualifying foreigners after a longer residency period.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of the following is a classic argument in favour of universal adult suffrage over a restricted (property-based) franchise?
options: It reflects the democratic principle that legitimate government rests on the consent of all adult citizens regardless of property, gender, or income
It ensures that only the wealthy classes determine government policy
It reduces the total number of eligible voters to a manageable minority
It guarantees a one-party system will always emerge victorious
questions.explanation: Universal adult suffrage rests on the democratic principle that political legitimacy flows from the consent of the entire adult citizenry rather than a propertied or otherwise restricted minority.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The First-Past-The-Post system tends to produce a disproportionality between votes cast and seats won mainly because
options: it requires an absolute majority of fifty percent plus one in every constituency before any seat can be allocated
the candidate with a simple plurality wins the constituency outright, so votes cast for losing candidates nationwide do not translate into any seats
it distributes seats strictly in proportion to each party's national vote share
it abolishes the concept of constituencies entirely
questions.explanation: Because only the candidate with the most votes in each single-member constituency wins the seat, votes for all other candidates are effectively 'wasted', creating a mismatch between national vote share and seats won.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Proportional representation is generally criticised on the grounds that it
options: always produces a decisive two-party system with strong, stable single-party majorities
can result in fragmented legislatures and unstable coalition governments due to the proliferation of smaller parties
makes it impossible for any minority party to win a single seat
eliminates the need for elections altogether
questions.explanation: Because proportional representation allocates seats closely to vote share, it tends to allow many smaller parties into the legislature, often necessitating unstable multi-party coalitions to form a government.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of the following best distinguishes a one-party system from a dominant-party democracy in which one party wins repeatedly?
options: A one-party system always guarantees free and fair competitive elections
A dominant-party democracy has no elections whatsoever

In a one-party system, the law or practice prohibits the formation or effective competition of rival parties, whereas in a dominant-party democracy other parties are legally free to contest and can, in principle, win power
There is no distinction; both terms describe identical arrangements
questions.explanation: A one-party system legally bars or effectively suppresses opposition parties, while a dominant-party democracy permits genuine multiparty competition even though one party consistently wins.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A major functional difference between a political party and a pressure group is that
options: a pressure group always has a wider and more general policy programme than a political party
a political party seeks to capture governmental power by contesting and winning elections, while a pressure group seeks to influence government policy without itself seeking to form the government
only pressure groups are permitted to sponsor candidates in elections
political parties cannot legally exist in a democracy
questions.explanation: Political parties aim to win elections and directly control the machinery of government, whereas pressure groups aim only to influence policy from outside without seeking to govern themselves.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: An 'electoral college' system, as historically used in some indirect presidential elections, is best described as one in which
options: ordinary citizens cast votes directly and exclusively for the president with no intermediary body
military officers select the head of state
the legislature alone appoints the president without any popular vote
citizens vote for delegates or electors who are then formally responsible for electing the president
questions.explanation: An electoral college system interposes a body of electors, chosen through popular vote, between the citizenry and the final selection of the president, making the process indirect.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of the following best explains why an independent Electoral Commission is generally considered essential for credible elections?
options: It guarantees automatic victory for the ruling party
It eliminates the need for a legal framework governing elections
Its independence from the incumbent executive helps ensure impartial conduct of registration, voting, collation and declaration of results, enhancing public confidence in the process
It is responsible solely for drafting the national budget
questions.explanation: An electoral body's independence from the sitting government is crucial to ensuring impartial administration of the electoral process, which in turn builds public and stakeholder confidence in the results.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Public opinion is best distinguished from propaganda in that public opinion
options: is identical in meaning to propaganda
is always manufactured directly by the government in power
cannot be measured or studied by any scientific method

is the genuine, aggregated view of the public on an issue formed through open discussion and access to information, while propaganda is a deliberate, often one-sided attempt to manipulate opinion in a particular direction
questions.explanation: Public opinion reflects the collective views citizens form through relatively open deliberation, whereas propaganda involves a deliberate, engineered effort to shape opinion, often through selective or misleading information.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: In a multi-party system with proportional representation, coalition government most commonly arises because
options: a single party wins an outright majority of legislative seats
no single party secures an outright majority of seats, requiring two or more parties to combine to command legislative confidence
the constitution bans any party from forming a government alone
elections are held only once every twenty years
questions.explanation: Under proportional systems, seats are often widely spread among several parties, so no party alone commands a majority, making coalition-building necessary to form a stable government.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The principle of political neutrality expected of career civil servants means that they are expected to
options: serve loyally and impartially whichever government is constitutionally in power, without regard to their personal political convictions
openly campaign for the ruling party during elections
resign automatically whenever a new government is elected
refuse to implement any policy they personally disagree with
questions.explanation: Political neutrality requires civil servants to serve any duly constituted government impartially and loyally, implementing its policies regardless of the servants' own political leanings.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Anonymity, as a traditional characteristic of the civil service, refers to the principle that
options: civil servants cannot be identified by any official designation
civil servants must conceal their salaries from the public
the names of all civil servants are permanently kept secret from other government departments
civil servants' individual advice and roles in policy formulation remain officially unattributed, with ministers publicly accountable for departmental decisions
questions.explanation: Anonymity means individual civil servants generally do not publicly take credit or blame for policy advice; instead, the responsible minister bears public accountability for departmental actions.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of the following is the most significant distinction between a public corporation and a government ministry/department?
options: A public corporation is a semi-autonomous body with a separate legal personality established by statute to run a specific enterprise, while a ministry is a direct arm of the central civil service under a minister
A ministry can be sued in its own name while a public corporation cannot
A public corporation cannot employ any staff
A ministry generates its own independent revenue while a public corporation depends entirely on the treasury
questions.explanation: Public corporations are created by specific enabling statutes as separate legal entities with a measure of operational autonomy, unlike ministries, which are integral parts of the civil service directly under ministerial control.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: One commonly cited justification for establishing public corporations rather than leaving certain services to purely private enterprise is that
options: they allow government to provide essential services or manage strategic/natural monopoly sectors (like utilities) in the public interest rather than for private profit alone
public corporations guarantee higher profits than private companies in every case
public corporations are exempt from all forms of government oversight
private companies are constitutionally prohibited from operating in any sector
questions.explanation: Public corporations are often established to manage services in the public interest, particularly natural monopolies or strategic sectors, ensuring broader access rather than being driven purely by private profit motives.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Bureaucratic red tape, as a criticism of the civil service, refers primarily to
options: the political neutrality expected of career officials
a formal system of promoting civil servants purely on merit
excessive procedural formality, rigid rules and slow administrative processes that hinder efficient service delivery
the anonymity traditionally accorded to civil servants
questions.explanation: Red tape describes excessive adherence to rigid rules and procedures that slows decision-making and service delivery, a commonly cited weakness of large bureaucracies.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of the following mechanisms best exemplifies external legislative control over the civil service and public corporations?
options: A corporation's board approving its own annual budget without any external review
A permanent secretary issuing internal departmental circulars
A minister privately reprimanding a junior civil servant
The Public Accounts Committee scrutinising public expenditure through audited accounts and summoning officials to account for spending
questions.explanation: Legislative oversight bodies such as the Public Accounts Committee provide an external check by scrutinising audited public expenditure and holding officials accountable, distinct from purely internal administrative control.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A defining feature distinguishing the pre-colonial Hausa-Fulani political system from the pre-colonial Igbo system was that the Hausa-Fulani system was
options: organised without any reference to Islamic law
entirely republican with no hereditary rulers of any kind
based on universal adult suffrage for selecting the Emir
a centralised, hierarchical emirate structure with the Emir at the apex exercising both political and religious authority, unlike the largely decentralised, acephalous Igbo structure
questions.explanation: The Hausa-Fulani emirate system was highly centralised and hierarchical under an Emir who combined political and religious (Islamic) authority, in sharp contrast to the decentralised, largely stateless Igbo system.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: In the pre-colonial Hausa-Fulani administrative hierarchy, the official known as the Waziri primarily served as
options: the chief tax collector responsible only for farm produce
the head of the emirate's cavalry forces exclusively
the Emir's chief adviser and vizier, coordinating the affairs of the emirate on the Emir's behalf
an elected village head with no connection to the emirate palace
questions.explanation: The Waziri functioned as the Emir's principal adviser and administrative coordinator, overseeing the general affairs of the emirate under the Emir's authority.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: In the pre-colonial Yoruba political system, the Oyomesi council served primarily to
options: act purely as a ceremonial body with no political function
serve exclusively as a military command unit
collect taxes on behalf of neighbouring kingdoms
select, install, and where necessary check or even depose an Alaafin who ruled tyrannically, thus acting as a constitutional constraint on royal power
questions.explanation: The Oyomesi, led by the Bashorun, had the constitutional power to select and install the Alaafin and could compel an oppressive ruler to abdicate, functioning as a check on monarchical excess in old Oyo.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The pre-colonial Igbo political system is best described by political scientists as
options: a rigidly centralised monarchy under a single paramount king
a colonial creation with no indigenous roots
an absolute theocracy governed solely by priests
a fundamentally acephalous (stateless) system in which authority was diffused among village councils, age-grades, lineage heads and title-holders
questions.explanation: Unlike the centralised Hausa-Fulani emirates or Yoruba kingdoms, most pre-colonial Igbo communities lacked a single paramount ruler, instead diffusing authority across village assemblies, age-grades and lineage-based institutions.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The Ozo title society among the pre-colonial Igbo functioned mainly as a mechanism for
options: conferring formal military conscription duties on all young men
granting social status, prestige and a voice in community decision-making to title-holders who had demonstrated wealth, integrity and achievement
replacing the age-grade system entirely
administering colonial taxation on behalf of the British
questions.explanation: The Ozo title conferred social prestige and a recognised role in communal governance on accomplished individuals, functioning as an achievement-based mechanism for acquiring authority in the absence of hereditary kingship.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Age-grade organisations in pre-colonial Igbo society served primarily to
options: select the paramount Igbo king for the entire ethnic group
organise members of similar age cohorts for communal labour, defence, and the enforcement of communal decisions and discipline
administer indirect rule on behalf of British colonial officers from the outset
collect customs duties at regional borders
questions.explanation: Age-grades grouped people of similar age for cooperative tasks such as communal labour, security and enforcing the decisions of village assemblies, forming part of the diffused Igbo governance structure.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Among the pre-colonial Yoruba, the Alaafin of Oyo's authority, though extensive, was constitutionally limited chiefly by
options: an elected national assembly modelled on the British Parliament
the Oyomesi and the Ifa oracle (through the Are Ona Kakanfo and religious functionaries), which could check or force the abdication of an unpopular Alaafin
the absence of any council or advisory body around the throne
a written constitution imposed by neighbouring Bini kingdom
questions.explanation: The Alaafin's power was checked by the Oyomesi council and complemented by religious and military office holders; a ruler who lost the confidence of these bodies could be compelled to abdicate.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which statement best captures a key similarity between the pre-colonial Yoruba and Hausa-Fulani political systems, distinguishing both from the Igbo system?
options: Both systems rejected any role for councils of chiefs or advisers
Both systems entirely lacked any hereditary component in succession
Both systems were based on written constitutions drafted before colonial contact
Both Yoruba and Hausa-Fulani systems featured centralised monarchies with an identifiable paramount ruler, unlike the largely decentralised Igbo political structure
questions.explanation: Despite differences in detail, both the Yoruba (Alaafin) and Hausa-Fulani (Emir) systems were centralised monarchies with a recognisable paramount ruler, contrasting with the diffused authority of the largely acephalous Igbo system.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Lord Lugard's system of Indirect Rule was fundamentally premised on the idea that
options: the British would abolish all existing indigenous political institutions and replace them entirely with British-style councils
each colony would immediately be granted full self-government
colonial administration would be conducted through existing indigenous rulers and institutions, who would implement British policies under the supervision of colonial Residents
traditional rulers would be stripped of any judicial or tax-collection functions
questions.explanation: Indirect Rule used existing traditional rulers and institutions as the local agents of colonial administration, working under British supervision, rather than dismantling indigenous authority structures outright.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Indirect Rule was applied with relative ease in Northern Nigeria mainly because
options: the existing centralised Hausa-Fulani emirate structure, with its established hierarchy of Emirs and administrative officials, provided a ready-made framework the British could work through
the region had no indigenous political institutions at all before colonial contact
the Northern peoples unanimously rejected any form of traditional authority
the region was governed directly by British officials with no involvement of local rulers whatsoever
questions.explanation: The pre-existing centralised emirate system in the North, with its clear hierarchy under Emirs, offered the British an established administrative framework well-suited to Indirect Rule.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Indirect Rule faced its greatest structural difficulty in Eastern Nigeria mainly because
options: the Igbo areas already had powerful paramount kings comparable to the Hausa-Fulani Emirs
the Igbo people refused to pay any form of taxation under any system

the largely acephalous, decentralised nature of Igbo political organisation meant there were no obvious centralised chiefs through whom the British could rule, leading to the artificial imposition of 'Warrant Chiefs'
the British had no colonial presence in Eastern Nigeria at all
questions.explanation: Because Igbo communities generally lacked centralised chieftaincy, the British artificially created 'Warrant Chiefs' to serve as intermediaries, a mismatch that provoked resentment and contributed to unrest such as the 1929 Aba Women's Riot.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Compared to the British policy of Indirect Rule, French colonial policy in West Africa is generally distinguished by its emphasis on
options: abolishing all forms of taxation in its colonies
an identical reliance on existing traditional emirs and chiefs to govern autonomously
granting immediate independence to all French colonies before 1900
assimilation, aiming to make colonial subjects culturally French citizens through direct administration, rather than governing extensively through indigenous institutions
questions.explanation: French colonial policy favoured direct rule and assimilation, seeking to integrate colonial subjects into French culture and citizenship, in contrast to Britain's greater reliance on indirect governance through existing indigenous authorities.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The Warrant Chief system introduced in South-Eastern Nigeria is best understood as
options: an artificial colonial creation appointing individuals, often without traditional legitimacy, as 'chiefs' holding a warrant from the British to administer local government and native courts
a faithful continuation of pre-existing Igbo chieftaincy institutions
a system exclusively used in the Hausa-Fulani emirates
a purely religious office with no administrative powers
questions.explanation: Because the Igbo lacked centralised chiefs, the British issued warrants conferring artificial chieftaincy authority on selected individuals, who often lacked genuine traditional legitimacy, to serve colonial administrative purposes.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The 1929 Aba Women's Riot is most directly linked to which colonial policy grievance?
options: Opposition to the introduction of universal adult suffrage
Fears that the colonial administration's counting of people and property (associated with Warrant Chiefs) signalled an impending direct taxation of women
A dispute over the location of the colonial capital
Rejection of the Richards Constitution's regional structure
questions.explanation: The riot was sparked by fears among Igbo and Ibibio women that a colonial census exercise, conducted through Warrant Chiefs, was a prelude to taxing women, reflecting deep resentment of the imposed Warrant Chief system.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Nationalist movements such as the NCNC emerged in colonial Nigeria mainly as a reaction against
options: excessive indigenous self-governance granted too early by the British
colonial exploitation, exclusion of Nigerians from meaningful political participation, and denial of self-determination, which spurred demands for constitutional reform and independence
the total absence of any British colonial presence in Nigeria
an oversupply of Nigerian representation in the colonial legislature
questions.explanation: Nationalist agitation grew out of grievances over colonial economic exploitation, racial discrimination, and exclusion from real political power, driving demands for greater self-government and eventual independence.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A major long-term political consequence of British colonial administration frequently cited by historians is that it
options: created a perfectly unified and homogeneous Nigerian national identity before independence
eliminated all forms of chieftaincy and traditional authority permanently

amalgamated diverse ethnic nationalities into a single territorial unit in 1914 without adequately integrating them, sowing seeds of the regional and ethnic tensions that shaped post-independence politics
established an immediate fully democratic federal constitution in 1900
questions.explanation: The 1914 amalgamation of the Northern and Southern Protectorates joined diverse peoples into one colony for administrative convenience without deep integration, a legacy widely blamed for post-independence regional and ethnic tensions.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The Clifford Constitution of 1922 is chiefly significant in Nigerian constitutional history for
options: introducing the principle of federalism to Nigeria for the first time
introducing the elective principle, allowing Lagos and Calabar to elect a limited number of members to the Legislative Council
granting full internal self-government to the Eastern Region
abolishing the Legislative Council entirely
questions.explanation: The Clifford Constitution's landmark innovation was introducing the elective principle, permitting a small number of Legislative Council members to be elected by voters in Lagos and Calabar, a first for British West Africa.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which feature most distinguishes the Richards Constitution of 1946 from the earlier Clifford Constitution of 1922?
options: The Richards Constitution introduced regionalism by creating separate Houses of Assembly for the Northern, Western and Eastern regions, laying groundwork for eventual federalism
The Richards Constitution abolished the Legislative Council altogether
The Richards Constitution granted Nigeria full independence
The Richards Constitution removed all Nigerians from the Legislative Council
questions.explanation: Governor Arthur Richards's 1946 Constitution introduced regional Houses of Assembly for the North, West and East, a significant step toward the federal structure Nigeria would later adopt.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The Macpherson Constitution of 1951 is chiefly noted for
options: introducing a more representative structure with an enlarged central legislature and regional Houses of Assembly/Chiefs with greater Nigerian participation, though it soon proved unworkable due to regional tensions
abolishing regional legislatures entirely in favour of a single central assembly
granting Nigeria a republican status with an executive president
being the constitution under which Nigeria became independent
questions.explanation: The Macpherson Constitution expanded Nigerian participation through an enlarged central legislature and regional assemblies, but its ambiguous federal-unitary structure provoked crises that necessitated further constitutional revision.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The Lyttelton Constitution of 1954 is chiefly significant for
options: abolishing the regions and re-establishing a fully unitary system
formally establishing a federal system of government for Nigeria with clearly defined powers for the central and regional governments
granting Nigeria independence from British rule
introducing the Federal Character Principle for the first time
questions.explanation: The Lyttelton Constitution of 1954 formally converted Nigeria into a federation, clearly demarcating powers between the central government and the three regions, resolving tensions left unresolved under Macpherson.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The most fundamental change introduced by the 1963 Republican Constitution, compared with the 1960 Independence Constitution, was that
options: Nigeria became a republic, replacing the British monarch as head of state with a ceremonial Nigerian President, while retaining the Westminster parliamentary framework
Nigeria adopted a presidential system of government for the first time
Nigeria abolished federalism and became a unitary state
the regions were dissolved and replaced with states
questions.explanation: The 1963 Constitution's key change was severing the constitutional link to the British Crown by making Nigeria a republic with an indigenous ceremonial President, while the parliamentary system of government itself was retained.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which statement correctly distinguishes the 1979 Constitution from the 1963 Republican Constitution?
options: The 1979 Constitution retained the Westminster parliamentary model unchanged from 1963
The 1979 Constitution replaced the parliamentary system with an American-style presidential system featuring an executive President elected independently of the legislature
The 1979 Constitution restored the British monarch as head of state
The 1979 Constitution abolished the federal system in favour of a unitary one
questions.explanation: The 1979 Constitution marked Nigeria's shift from the parliamentary system inherited from Britain to a presidential system modelled on the United States, with a separately elected executive President.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A notable innovation first entrenched in the 1979 Constitution, and retained in the 1999 Constitution, aimed at managing Nigeria's ethnic diversity in appointments is
options: the abolition of state creation
the Federal Character Principle, requiring that the composition of government and its agencies reflect the diversity of the country to promote national unity
the requirement that only military officers can hold the office of President
the restriction of citizenship to a single ethnic group
questions.explanation: The Federal Character Principle, introduced in the 1979 Constitution and preserved thereafter, mandates that appointments and government composition reflect Nigeria's federal diversity to avoid the domination of any one group.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The 1999 Constitution, under which the Fourth Republic currently operates, is best described as having
options: restored and continued the presidential federal system introduced by the 1979 Constitution, following prolonged military rule
returned Nigeria to a parliamentary system similar to the First Republic
established Nigeria as a unitary state for the first time
abolished the office of state governor
questions.explanation: The 1999 Constitution largely re-adopted the presidential federal framework of the 1979 Constitution, marking the transition from prolonged military rule to the current Fourth Republic.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of the following correctly orders these Nigerian constitutions chronologically from earliest to latest?
options: Clifford, Richards, Macpherson, Lyttelton
Richards, Clifford, Macpherson, Lyttelton
Macpherson, Clifford, Lyttelton, Richards
Lyttelton, Macpherson, Richards, Clifford
questions.explanation: The correct chronological order is the Clifford Constitution (1922), Richards Constitution (1946), Macpherson Constitution (1951), and Lyttelton Constitution (1954).

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A major criticism levelled at the Macpherson Constitution of 1951, which ultimately led to its early replacement, was that
options: it granted Nigeria full independence too abruptly
it abolished traditional rulers from all forms of participation in government

its ambiguous division of powers between the centre and the regions, combined with rising regional and ethnic rivalries, made the system of government unworkable, notably contributing to a crisis in the Western House of Assembly
it introduced too rigid a federal structure that left the regions no power at all
questions.explanation: The Macpherson Constitution's unclear federal-unitary balance and rising regional political rivalry, exemplified by the 1953 crisis in the Western Region assembly, exposed its unworkability and prompted the move to the more clearly federal Lyttelton Constitution.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The First Republic (1963-1966) collapsed mainly as a result of
options: a peaceful and orderly transition to a presidential system
an amicable merger of all political parties into one national party
a combination of disputed elections, regional and ethnic political rivalries, and a breakdown of law and order culminating in the January 1966 military coup
the abolition of the federal system by consensus among the regions
questions.explanation: The First Republic's collapse resulted from deep regional/ethnic political rivalries, disputed elections (notably in the Western Region), and widespread instability, which culminated in the military takeover of January 1966.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The Second Republic (1979-1983) was terminated by which event?
options: The December 31, 1983 military coup led by Major-General Muhammadu Buhari, citing widespread electoral malpractice and economic mismanagement
A peaceful handover to a newly elected civilian government
A constitutional amendment abolishing elections
Nigeria's voluntary withdrawal from the Commonwealth
questions.explanation: The Second Republic ended when the military, led by Major-General Muhammadu Buhari, overthrew the Shagari administration on December 31, 1983, citing electoral fraud and economic mismanagement.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The short-lived Third Republic is most closely associated with
options: the peaceful completion of a full four-year presidential term by an elected civilian government
the adoption of a new republican constitution abolishing federalism
the annulment of the June 12, 1993 presidential election, widely believed to have been won by Chief M.K.O. Abiola, which plunged the country into political crisis
Nigeria's first ever multi-party local government elections
questions.explanation: The Third Republic is chiefly remembered for the annulment of the June 12, 1993 presidential election, widely regarded as Nigeria's freest, which Abiola was believed to have won, triggering a major political crisis.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Under military rule in Nigeria, the highest ruling organ combining legislative and executive authority was typically known as the
options: National Assembly
Federal Executive Council acting alone with no military input
Supreme Military Council or Provisional Ruling Council/Armed Forces Ruling Council, depending on the era
Council of State comprised solely of civilian ex-presidents
questions.explanation: Under successive military regimes, supreme authority combining legislative and executive powers was vested in bodies variously named the Supreme Military Council, Armed Forces Ruling Council, or Provisional Ruling Council.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: During periods of military rule in Nigeria, laws were typically enacted through
options: Decrees issued by the ruling military council, which took precedence over and could override the suspended constitution
ordinary Acts passed by an elected National Assembly
Regulations passed exclusively by the judiciary
referenda held nationwide before every new law
questions.explanation: Military governments legislated by decree, issued by the ruling council, and these decrees typically had overriding legal force even above the (usually suspended) constitution.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A commonly cited structural weakness of military rule in Nigeria, distinct from mere policy failures, is that it
options: guaranteed permanent, uninterrupted economic growth
strengthened an independent judiciary beyond civilian standards
concentrated legislative, executive and often judicial-oversight power in an unelected body, undermining accountability, the rule of law, and constitutional checks and balances
expanded civil liberties and freedom of the press beyond civilian norms
questions.explanation: Military regimes fused legislative and executive power in an unelected ruling council and often suspended or subordinated the constitution, weakening accountability mechanisms and the separation of powers fundamental to constitutional government.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The transition programme that led to the Fourth Republic in 1999 was initiated under which military head of state?
options: General Yakubu Gowon
General Abdulsalami Abubakar
General Sani Abacha
General Ibrahim Babangida
questions.explanation: General Abdulsalami Abubakar, who assumed power after General Abacha's death in 1998, oversaw the swift transition programme that culminated in the 1999 return to civilian rule under Olusegun Obasanjo.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of the following best explains why military intervention was historically able to recur multiple times in Nigerian politics (1966, 1975, 1983, 1985, 1993)?
options: Nigeria's constitution explicitly authorised periodic military takeovers every decade
The Nigerian populace voted directly for military rule in national referenda

Recurring problems such as weak institutionalisation of democratic norms, electoral malpractice, economic crisis, and elite political rivalry created conditions military factions repeatedly exploited to justify intervention
The United Nations mandated military rule as a condition of Nigeria's membership
questions.explanation: Repeated military takeovers were driven by recurring weaknesses in Nigeria's civilian governance — disputed elections, economic mismanagement, and elite rivalries — which military actors invoked to justify seizing power.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of the following is most accurately identified as an achievement often credited to military regimes in Nigeria, despite their authoritarian character?
options: Strengthening multi-party competition and legislative oversight
Entrenching judicial review over executive decrees
Expanding an independent and unrestrained press
Executing major infrastructural and unification projects, such as the creation of additional states and completion of national infrastructure, partly enabled by centralised decision-making
questions.explanation: Military regimes are often credited with executing large infrastructural projects and administrative reforms like state creation swiftly, aided by centralised command, even though such regimes curtailed democratic institutions.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: A defining feature of Nigeria's Fourth Republic since 1999, distinguishing it from earlier republics, is
options: the total absence of any elections since 1999
its adoption of a parliamentary rather than presidential system
its unprecedented duration as the longest unbroken period of civilian, constitutional government in Nigeria's post-independence history
the abolition of the 36-state structure
questions.explanation: The Fourth Republic, running continuously since 1999, represents Nigeria's longest sustained period of uninterrupted civilian constitutional government, unlike the shorter First, Second and Third Republics.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The transition from military to civilian rule typically in Nigeria's history involved which sequence of steps?
options: Immediate handover without any elections or constitutional preparation

A transition programme involving activities such as constitution drafting/review, voter registration, party formation, and phased elections (local, state, then federal) culminating in inauguration of an elected government
Permanent retention of power by the military with no elections planned
Direct appointment of a civilian president by the United Nations
questions.explanation: Nigerian transition programmes typically followed a phased sequence: reviewing or drafting a constitution, registering voters, forming and registering parties, and holding graduated elections before finally handing over to an elected civilian government.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which statement best distinguishes the causes of the January 1966 coup from those commonly cited for the December 1983 coup?
options: The January 1966 coup was caused solely by economic recession while the 1983 coup was caused solely by an external war
Both coups occurred for identical reasons with no distinguishing context

The January 1966 coup is often linked to regional/ethnic political rivalry and the crisis following disputed regional elections, while the 1983 coup is more commonly attributed to widespread electoral malpractice in the 1983 elections and severe economic mismanagement
Neither coup had any connection to electoral or political crisis
questions.explanation: The 1966 coup arose largely from ethnic and regional political tensions and the Western Region crisis, whereas the 1983 coup was driven chiefly by allegations of massive electoral fraud in the 1983 polls and deepening economic troubles.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of the following best expresses the concept of 'Afrocentrism' as a stated principle of Nigeria's foreign policy?
options: Nigeria prioritises its relations with Western powers above all African concerns
Nigeria refuses to engage in diplomatic relations with any non-African country
Africa is regarded as the centre-piece of Nigeria's foreign policy, with the promotion of African unity, decolonisation and development given primary emphasis
Nigeria's foreign policy is determined exclusively by the United Nations Security Council
questions.explanation: Afrocentrism holds that Africa is the primary focus of Nigeria's external relations, with Nigeria positioning itself as a champion of African unity, decolonisation, and development on the continent.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Nigeria's foreign policy principle of 'non-alignment' during the Cold War era referred to its stance of
options: formally allying with the Soviet bloc against Western powers
joining NATO as a full member state
refusing to align permanently with either the Western (capitalist) or Eastern (communist) bloc, instead pursuing an independent foreign policy based on national interest
severing all diplomatic relations with both blocs simultaneously
questions.explanation: Non-alignment meant Nigeria avoided formal, permanent commitment to either Cold War bloc, choosing instead to engage both sides pragmatically according to its own national interests.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Nigeria's role in the anti-apartheid struggle, particularly its support for the African National Congress and financial contributions through bodies it helped fund, most directly reflects which foreign policy principle?
options: Non-interference in the internal affairs of other states under all circumstances
Priority of bilateral trade relations over political solidarity
Strict neutrality on all matters concerning Southern Africa
Commitment to African unity, decolonisation and the eradication of racial discrimination and colonialism on the continent
questions.explanation: Nigeria's vigorous support for South Africa's liberation, including funding and diplomatic pressure against apartheid, exemplified its foreign policy commitment to decolonisation and combating racial oppression across Africa.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of the following is the most accurate description of Nigeria's foreign policy principle of respect for the sovereign equality and territorial integrity of all states?
options: Nigeria reserves the right to unilaterally alter the borders of neighbouring states
Nigeria only respects the sovereignty of fellow Commonwealth members
Nigeria commits to recognising the legal equality and territorial boundaries of other states and generally refrains from interfering in their internal affairs
Nigeria's principle applies solely to relations with the United States
questions.explanation: This principle commits Nigeria to recognising other states as legal equals regardless of size or power, respecting their territorial boundaries, and generally avoiding interference in their domestic affairs.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Nigeria's leadership in establishing the ECOWAS Monitoring Group (ECOMOG) in the late 1980s was most directly a response to the need to
options: create a customs union eliminating tariffs among West African states
provide a peacekeeping and peace-enforcement force to address civil conflict, notably in Liberia, threatening regional stability in West Africa
establish a single West African currency
coordinate agricultural research among member states
questions.explanation: ECOMOG was created primarily as a peacekeeping/peace-enforcement mechanism, with Nigeria providing the bulk of troops and leadership, initially to intervene in the Liberian civil war and later in Sierra Leone.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which best distinguishes the mandates of ECOWAS and the African Union (AU)?
options: ECOWAS is a global organisation while the AU is limited to West Africa
The AU has no role in peacekeeping while ECOWAS's sole mandate is peacekeeping

ECOWAS is a sub-regional body focused on economic integration and, increasingly, security in West Africa, while the AU is a continental body promoting unity, peace and development across all of Africa
ECOWAS and the AU are simply two names for the same organisation
questions.explanation: ECOWAS is a sub-regional body concentrating on West African economic integration and, over time, security cooperation, whereas the AU is the continental body pursuing broader pan-African unity, peace, and development goals.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Which of the following is most accurately described as a determinant, rather than a stated principle, of Nigeria's foreign policy?
options: Nigeria's size, population, natural resource endowment (including oil), and geo-strategic location in West Africa, which shape its capacity and orientation in external relations
Respect for the sovereign equality of states
Peaceful settlement of international disputes
Non-alignment in global power blocs
questions.explanation: Determinants of foreign policy are underlying factors such as a country's size, resources, and geography that shape its external orientation, as distinct from the declared normative principles that guide policy conduct.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Nigeria's foreign policy has generally treated relations with major world powers such as the United States and the United Kingdom on the basis of
options: mutual respect for sovereignty and pursuit of national interest, including trade, investment and diplomatic cooperation, without permanent alignment to any bloc
unconditional subordination to those powers' foreign policy positions
complete severance of diplomatic and economic ties
automatic military alliance obligations
questions.explanation: Nigeria has generally sought pragmatic, mutually respectful relations with major powers, prioritising national interest in trade and diplomacy while avoiding permanent bloc alignment.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The Commonwealth of Nations, of which Nigeria is a member, is best described as an association whose members are primarily
options: nations located solely within continental Europe
exclusively the founding members of the United Nations
only Francophone West African states
states that were once part of, or have historical ties to, the former British Empire, cooperating on shared values such as democracy and development
questions.explanation: The Commonwealth is a voluntary association mainly comprising former British colonies and territories, cooperating on shared goals like democracy, human rights and development.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: Nigeria's suspension from the Commonwealth between 1995 and 1999 was most directly triggered by
options: the execution of Ken Saro-Wiwa and other Ogoni activists under the Abacha military regime, which drew international condemnation over human rights abuses
Nigeria's withdrawal from the United Nations
Nigeria's refusal to participate in ECOWAS peacekeeping
a border dispute with Cameroon over the Bakassi Peninsula
questions.explanation: The Commonwealth suspended Nigeria's membership in 1995 primarily in protest against the Abacha regime's execution of Ken Saro-Wiwa and other Ogoni rights activists despite international appeals for clemency.

questions.subject: Government
questions.text: The peaceful settlement of the Bakassi Peninsula dispute between Nigeria and Cameroon, following a ruling by the International Court of Justice, most directly illustrates Nigeria's foreign policy commitment to
options: respect for international law and peaceful settlement of disputes through recognised international judicial mechanisms
unilateral military resolution of territorial disputes
permanent rejection of ICJ jurisdiction over African disputes
withdrawal from all international courts and organisations
questions.explanation: Nigeria's acceptance of and eventual compliance with the ICJ's 2002 ruling on the Bakassi Peninsula demonstrated its foreign policy commitment to resolving international disputes peacefully through established legal mechanisms rather than force.
